case_name: VIP Products, LLC v. Jack Daniel's Properties, Inc.

case_name: Jack Daniel's Properties, Inc. v. VIP Products LLC
senior_mark: JACK DANIEL'S (word marks and bottle trade dress)
notes: Rogers test inapplicable when the accused use is a source identifier; parody/noncommercial exclusion to dilution does not cover source-identifying uses. Vacated 953 F.3d 1170 and remanded; no factor analysis. Sotomayor concurrence warns against uncritical weight on surveys in parody cases.

case_name: VIP Products, LLC v. Jack Daniel's Properties, Inc. (on remand)
senior_mark: JACK DANIEL'S (word marks and bottle trade dress)
senior_goods: Tennessee whiskey; licensed merchandise incl. dog products
quote_relatedness: The Court sees no reason to depart from its prior conclusion that the proximity of goods factor weighs in favor of Jack Daniel’s.
notes: Post-SCOTUS remand. Relatedness, channels (tips to JD but 'does not weigh heavily'), actual confusion (survey, limited weight) and buyer care still favored Jack Daniel's, but parody flipped similarity, strength and intent: NO likelihood of confusion. Court still found dilution by tarnishment (reversed by 9th Cir. 2026).

case_name: VIP Products, LLC v. Jack Daniel's Properties, Inc.
senior_mark: JACK DANIEL'S (word mark and registered bottle trade dress)
notes: Vacates tarnishment injunction; remands for judgment for VIP on dilution. Only 'Jack Daniel's' and registered trade dress proved famous; Bad Spaniels did not facially tarnish them. Confusion ruling for VIP (2025) not at issue. Net result of the saga: VIP prevails on both claims.

case_name: In-N-Out Burgers v. Smashburger IP Holder LLC
notes: No likelihood-of-confusion opinion located (not on CourtListener search results or GovInfo; CourtListener API rate-limited). case_name: Tiffany & Co. v. Costco Wholesale Corp.

case_name: Louis Vuitton Malletier S.A. v. Haute Diggity Dog, LLC

case_name: Starbucks Corp. v. Wolfe's Borough Coffee, Inc.

notes: Dilution by blurring only (confusion resolved in 2009). Starbucks marks famous; minimal similarity in marketplace context and weak actual association (Mitofsky phone survey: 30.5% first-thought 'Starbucks', 3.1% named Starbucks as possible source) => no likelihood of dilution.

case_name: Starbucks Corp. v. Wolfe's Borough Coffee, Inc.

case_name: Coach Services, Inc. v. Triumph Learning LLC
quote_relatedness: Although CSI’s COACH mark is famous for likelihood of confusion purposes, the unrelated nature of the parties’ goods and their different channels of trade weigh heavily against CSI.
notes: TTAB opposition appeal. Board found classes of consumers MAY overlap (favoring Coach) but goods unrelated and trade channels distinct. COACH famous for LOC purposes but NOT shown famous for dilution (fame_found=no is dilution fame). Remanded only on Triumph's acquired distinctiveness.

case_name: Vans, Inc. v. MSCHF Product Studio, Inc.

case_name: Rolex Watch USA, Inc. v. BeckerTime, L.L.C.

case_name: Hermès International v. Rothschild

case_name: Levi Strauss & Co. v. Abercrombie & Fitch Trading Co.
notes: Holds the 'identical or nearly identical' standard did not survive the TDRA; reverses and remands dilution judgment. No confusion factor analysis.

case_name: Kraft Foods Group Brands LLC v. Cracker Barrel Old Country Store, Inc.

case_name: FIJI Water Co. v. FIJI Mineral Water USA, LLC
senior_mark: FIJI (word mark and bottle trade dress)
quote_relatedness: It is undeniable that the products have the same uses and functions.

case_name: Moseley v. V Secret Catalogue, Inc.
notes: FTDA required actual dilution, not likelihood; mental association alone insufficient (prompted the TDRA 2006). Confusion claim lost below, not before the Court. Junior user is a single local store.

case_name: V Secret Catalogue, Inc. v. Moseley
notes: On remand under the TDRA: rebuttable presumption of tarnishment when a semantically associated mark is used to sell sex-related products; affirmed for Victoria's Secret.

case_name: Mattel, Inc. v. MCA Records, Inc.

case_name: Dr. Seuss Enterprises, L.P. v. ComicMix LLC

case_name: Tommy Hilfiger Licensing, Inc. v. Nature Labs, LLC

case_name: Kellogg Co. v. Toucan Golf, Inc.

case_name: Nautilus Group, Inc. v. ICON Health & Fitness, Inc.

case_name: Louis Vuitton Malletier v. Dooney & Bourke, Inc.

case_name: Christian Louboutin S.A. v. Yves Saint Laurent America Holding, Inc.

case_name: Pom Wonderful LLC v. Hubbard

case_name: Fortune Dynamic, Inc. v. Victoria's Secret Stores Brand Management, Inc.

case_name: Palm Bay Imports, Inc. v. Veuve Clicquot Ponsardin Maison Fondee en 1772

case_name: Multi Time Machine, Inc. v. Amazon.com, Inc.

case_name: Bose Corp. v. QSC Audio Products, Inc.

case_name: Louis Vuitton Malletier v. Burlington Coat Factory Warehouse Corp.

case_name: Rosetta Stone Ltd. v. Google, Inc.

notes: Vacated summary judgment on direct/contributory infringement and dilution. Disputed factors were intent, actual confusion (internal Google studies: 94% of users confused at least once) and consumer sophistication.

case_name: AutoZone, Inc. v. Tandy Corp.

case_name: A & H Sportswear, Inc. v. Victoria's Secret Stores, Inc.

case_name: GoTo.com, Inc. v. Walt Disney Co.

case_name: Playtex Products, Inc. v. Georgia-Pacific Corp.

Wet Ones called 'famous' in the strength (LOC) analysis; federal dilution failed for lack of actual dilution (Moseley).

case_name: Sullivan v. CBS Corp.

quote_relatedness: Skechers does not dispute that the proximity-of-goods factor favors finding a likelihood of confusion. The Court agrees, and finds that the proximity-of-goods factor weighs moderately in favor of a likelihood of confusion.
notes: Bench-trial findings of fact and conclusions of law; judgment for Skechers on all claims (Doc. 186). Page 22: same class of purchasers, same marketing channels (retail stores, catalogues, e-commerce), similar $55-$70 prices. Marks dissimilar, 0% survey confusion. Scanned PDF read as page images; quote transcribed by hand (automated check cannot run). Trade dress claims had been dismissed at summary judgment.

case_name: Stone Brewing Co. v. MillerCoors LLC
quote_relatedness: Regarding the proximity of the goods, both products are beer. While MillerCoors rightly points out the beers make up very different segments of the beer industry, the jury was entitled to conclude the goods were related by participating the same general industry.
notes: Order denying MillerCoors's renewed JMOL after the jury verdict for Stone. Relatedness label rests on jury-review language ('the jury was entitled to conclude the goods were related'); the judge says he would have found no confusion as fact-finder. Channels not separately discussed.

case_name: adidas-Salomon AG v. Target Corp.
senior_mark: adidas THREE-STRIPE mark; Superstar trade dress
junior_mark: four-stripe B.U.M. shoes sold at Target
quote_relatedness: This factor favors adidas since defendants are using a four stripe design on a nearly identical product of athletic shoes.
notes: District judge adopts magistrate's findings; Target/B.U.M. motion for summary judgment denied (mixed = issues go to trial). Marketing channels and other factors 'lack any evidence and therefore do not bear on the analysis' (not_discussed). Triable issue on fame of the Superstar trade dress for dilution (not decided). Accused seller brand: Target.

case_name: Tempur Sealy International, Inc. v. Mattress Firm, Inc.
junior_mark: Tempur-Sealy marks on Mattress Firm web page and AdWords
quote_relatedness: Therefore, the court finds that the digits of confusion relating to the similarity of the two marks, the similarity of the products, the identity of the purchasers, and the identity of the advertising media, weigh in favor of a finding a likelihood of confusion.
notes: Former retailer using the manufacturer's marks to sell competing mattresses. Second PI motion granted in part (web page use limited to comparative advertising plus disclaimer); AdWords alone not enjoined. Channels label from the identity-of-purchasers and advertising-media digits.

case_name: Checkpoint Systems, Inc. v. Check Point Software Technologies, Inc.
quote_relatedness: Because the products serve different functions, and there is only “minimal overlap” in the product technology, it is unlikely consumers would be confused by the similar marks.
notes: Judgment for Check Point after bench trial affirmed. Different segments of corporate security; different trade shows, magazines and resellers ('do not market their products through the same trade channels'). Both parties sell mainly to businesses, not consumers; Qloo coverage may be thin.

case_name: Freedom Card, Inc. v. JPMorgan Chase & Co.
quote_relatedness: To reiterate, Chase was in the prime market, and UTN was in the sub-prime market (or the sub-sub-prime market as Chase suggests).
notes: Declaratory-judgment posture: Chase is plaintiff; labels oriented to UTN (senior, counterclaimant, reverse confusion). Summary judgment for Chase affirmed. Court relies on different target consumers (prime vs sub-prime); no separate goods-relatedness finding. UTN/FREEDOM CARD is not a known brand. Quote describes the purchaser split, not goods.

case_name: Hershey Co. v. Art Van Furniture, Inc.
senior_mark: HERSHEY'S chocolate bar wrapper trade dress
quote_relatedness: On the other hand, the lack of relatedness between the parties' goods and services, the difference in marketing channels used and varying degrees of care purchasers are likely to exercise when buying the parties' products, suggest that consumer confusion is unlikely.
notes: TRO/PI: infringement and unfair competition unlikely to succeed (unrelated goods, different marketing channels, different purchaser care); dilution by blurring likely, so relief granted on dilution only (mixed by claim). Hershey trade dress found famous and distinctive. Art Van is a regional (Michigan) furniture chain.

case_name: New York Stock Exchange, Inc. v. New York, New York Hotel, LLC
junior_mark: New York-New York casino's modified NYSE marks (MGM)
quote_relatedness: There is no evidence that NYSE and the Casino compete directly in any market or that NYSE plans to “bridge the gap” by entering the casino business.
notes: Summary judgment for the casino on infringement affirmed (no direct competition, no bridging the gap, humor). Dilution: dismissal affirmed for most marks (not inherently distinctive) but reversed for the facade logo, including tarnishment; mixed. NYSE described as 'famous in the business world and beyond' in background; dilution-level fame not decided.

case_name: Vital Pharmaceuticals, Inc. v. Monster Energy Co.
quote_relatedness: While Bang and Reign are not at all identical, they are both energy drinks that target health-conscious consumers. And they're both the kinds of products a consumer might attribute to a single source.
notes: Bench-trial judgment for Monster: Bang trade dress not inherently distinctive, no secondary meaning, and no likelihood of confusion (dissimilar designs, house marks, weak survey). Factors 3 (similarity of products) and 4 (trade channels and customers) favored VPX.

case_name: Vans, Inc. v. Walmart, Inc.
senior_mark: VANS Side Stripe; OLD SKOOL and SK8-HI trade dress
junior_mark: Walmart side-stripe sneakers (Wonder Nation and others)
quote_relatedness: Walmart concedes that "the parties' shoes are in proximity to each other."
notes: Preliminary injunction granted. Relatedness conceded by Walmart. Marketing channels held irrelevant because Vans argued only post-sale confusion ('does not weigh into the analysis').

case_name: Star Industries, Inc. v. Bacardi & Co.
quote_relatedness: Georgi 0 and Bacardi 0 are in moderate competitive proximity with one another.
notes: Judgment for Bacardi affirmed. Proximity 'moderate' and 'tempered' (distinct sub-markets of alcoholic beverages); the proximity discussion says vodka and rum are 'sold in the same stores to the same consumers' (channels label from that sentence). Five factors favored Bacardi. Quote reproduces the reporter's OCR ('0' for 'O'). Georgi is a low-price vodka brand.

case_name: Spangler Candy Co. v. Tootsie Roll Industries, LLC
quote_relatedness: Tootsie concedes the following factors weigh in Spangler's favor: "relatedness of the goods" and "marketing channels used."
notes: Preliminary injunction granted on packaging trade dress. Relatedness and marketing channels conceded by Tootsie; weak trade dress and no actual confusion, but intent and side-by-side shelving carried the result.

case_name: Tillamook Country Smoker, Inc. v. Tillamook County Creamery Ass'n
quote_relatedness: The court concludes that cheese and smoked meat snacks are particularly closely related.
notes: Declaratory-judgment posture: Smoker is plaintiff; labels oriented to the Creamery (senior, counterclaimant). Laches bars objection to TILLAMOOK COUNTRY SMOKER; TILLAMOOK JERKY held infringing on summary judgment (mixed). Sleekcraft troika favored the Creamery: same supermarkets, same shopping trip.

case_name: Therma-Scan, Inc. v. Thermoscan, Inc.
quote_relatedness: The two factors with the most relevance to the present case — the relatedness of the goods and services and the marketing channels used' — both weigh strongly against finding a likelihood of confusion.
notes: Summary judgment for Thermoscan affirmed. Goods use similar technology in very different ways and are marketed to different segments; a shared Internet presence is not a common marketing channel. Senior is a small Michigan clinic business (not a known brand); Thermoscan is a known consumer thermometer brand. Quote keeps the reporter's stray apostrophe.

case_name: Surfvivor Media, Inc. v. Survivor Productions
quote_relatedness: In this case, although both parties portray an outdoor theme, there is no material evidence in the record that customers are likely to associate the two products or conclude that the products come from the same source.
notes: Summary judgment for Survivor Productions affirmed. Relatedness favors Survivor; marketing channels 'slightly' favor Surfvivor (minor overlap in Hawaiian J.C. Penney stores). Senior is a small Hawaiian beach-products company (not a known brand).
